title: Clinical Guidance for Management of Adult Patients with Acute Respiratory Symptoms and Acute Bronchitis
author_or_organization: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India
date_uncertainty_note: National clinical guidance for respiratory infections in adult primary care.

passages.text: Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting inflammation of the large airways, overwhelmingly caused by respiratory viruses (influenza, parainfluenza, RSV, rhinovirus). The hallmark symptom is cough lasting between 1 to 3 weeks (median 18 days). Purulent sputum production occurs in roughly half of patients and represents desquamated bronchial epithelial cells and inflammatory cells rather than bacterial infection.

passages.section_heading: 2. Pertinent Negative Findings Distinguishing from Pneumonia
passages.text: In uncomplicated acute bronchitis, physiological vital signs remain essentially normal. Vital signs and physical examination show absence of high fever (temperature > 38.0°C), absence of tachypnea (respiratory rate > 24 breaths/min), absence of resting tachycardia (heart rate > 100 beats/min), and absence of focal chest signs (no bronchial breath sounds, egophony, or localized crackles). Normal vital signs effectively lower the probability of community-acquired pneumonia.

passages.section_heading: 3. Respiratory Red Flags Requiring Immediate Hospitalization
passages.text: Immediate hospital evaluation is indicated if the patient develops: resting dyspnea or acute shortness of breath, pulse oximetry SpO2 < 92% on room air, hemoptysis (coughing up gross blood), high-pitched inspiratory stridor, altered mental state, central cyanosis, or hemodynamic collapse. Patients with underlying severe COPD or immunocompromise require early clinician review.

Routine antibiotic treatment provides minimal clinical benefit for acute bronchitis in immunocompetent adults and contributes to antimicrobial resistance. Management is supportive: adequate oral hydration, honey or over-the-counter antitussives for cough relief, and inhaled short-acting beta-agonists only in patients with documented expiratory wheezing and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
